ports.use: Active/passive data channel and control channel. Plaintext — if a customer still uses it, the fix is SFTP, not a firewall rule.
Remote shell and file copy. First check when a Linux host 'cannot be reached' but pings: is sshd listening, is the key right, is fail2ban blocking you?
Plaintext remote terminal. Treat as a finding in any scan; it belongs in a legacy VLAN, never on the internet.
Mail relay. Most L1 mail tickets are port 25 blocked by the ISP/host, or a relay that refuses your IP.
UDP mostly, TCP for large answers and zone transfer. If name resolution fails, nothing else looks healthy.
Plain web. Redirects to 443 should be the only thing it serves; a login form on 80 is an audit finding.
Mail download, usually deletes from server. Explains 'mail disappeared from my phone but is on my laptop'.
Mail sync across devices. Wrong port or TLS mode is the usual Outlook 'cannot connect' cause.
TLS web. Certificate errors here are the most common 'site is down' call that is not a site outage.
Windows file shares. Blocked by most ISPs on purpose; never expose to the internet.
Remote desktop. Brute-forced constantly; if it must exist, it goes behind VPN or a gateway with MFA.

linux.what: Print working directory — confirms where a relative path will resolve before you run anything destructive.
List directory contents; -la shows permissions, owners and hidden files, which is where most 'file is missing' tickets end.
Change directory; no argument returns to the home directory.
Create a directory; -p creates parents in one step.
Print a file; the fastest way to read a small config or log without an editor.
Search text; -r walks a tree, -i ignores case, -n gives line numbers for the handover note.
Find files by name, age, size or permission — 'what changed in the last hour' is a find command.
Change permission bits; 644 files, 755 directories and scripts are the default starting point.
Change owner and group; a web server that cannot read its own document root is usually this.
List processes; aux or -ef shows the command line and the user, which identifies the runaway job.
Live process view; press M for memory, P for CPU, and read load average before blaming the application.
Run one command with elevated rights; -l shows what you are allowed to run without guessing.
Show interfaces and addresses; confirms the box has the address you think it has.
Show listening TCP/UDP sockets with process names; the single most useful 'is the service actually up' check.
Read the systemd journal; -u for one unit, -xe for recent failures with context, --since for a window.

windows.what: Address, gateway, DNS servers; /all also shows the DHCP server and lease, /flushdns clears a poisoned cache.
Reachability and latency; a reply proves the path, a timeout does not prove the host is down (ICMP may be blocked).
Current identity and groups; /groups shows whether the elevated token is actually present.
Running processes with PID and memory; /svc shows which services run inside each process.
List or manage local accounts; also the fastest check for a locked or disabled account.
PowerShell process objects; sort by CPU or working set and pipe to Select-Object for a readable top ten.
Service state and start type; a service set to Manual that should be Automatic is a classic reboot surprise.
Read classic Windows event logs (Application, System, Security) with -Newest and -EntryType filters.
Query any event channel with structured filters; the right tool for 'find every 4625 in the last hour'.

filters.use: Show only DNS queries and responses — the first filter in any 'name does not resolve' capture.
Show HTTP requests and responses; confirms whether the client ever sent the request.
Show TCP segments; combine with a port to isolate one conversation.
Show UDP datagrams; DHCP and DNS failures live here.
Show ping and ICMP errors; unreachable messages explain silent timeouts.
Show only connection attempts; distinguishes 'no route' from 'connection refused'.
Focus on one host in either direction; add tcp.port to narrow further.
Show DNS answers that failed (NXDOMAIN, SERVFAIL) — the proof for a resolver ticket.

eventIds.why: Baseline for who logged on where; logon type 3 (network) and 10 (RDP) tell different stories.
A burst is brute force or a stale service account; one every few minutes is often a scheduled task.
The audit trail for what actually ran; requires command-line auditing to be useful.
Any unexpected account creation is a containment decision, not a ticket to close.
Often an offboarding mistake or an attacker cleaning up; correlate with the HR leaver list.
Almost never legitimate on a production host. Treat as high severity until proven otherwise.

vulnerabilities.name: SQL Injection
vulnerabilities.fix: Parameterised queries or an ORM; never string concatenation, and never a WAF as the only fix.

vulnerabilities.name: XSS
vulnerabilities.fix: Output encoding at the sink plus a Content-Security-Policy; input filtering alone does not fix it.

vulnerabilities.name: Weak authentication
vulnerabilities.fix: MFA for remote and privileged access, lockout thresholds, and no shared accounts.

vulnerabilities.name: Misconfiguration
vulnerabilities.fix: Hardening baseline, remove default pages and sample apps, close unused ports, restrict management planes.

vulnerabilities.name: Outdated components
vulnerabilities.fix: Patch cadence with an owner, an inventory of versions, and a rollback plan.
